title: Wiesel and Abraham: Arguing with God
hook: Elie Wiesel, a survivor, wrote to bear witness and kept asking hard questions
carry: arguing with god is abraham's way of faith
tomorrow: a huge book, in a language you can't read. who opened it?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fackenheim's answer to catastrophe: candles in an ordinary kitchen, kept anyway. Keep living Jewishly. Today, a survivor who kept living, and kept asking.

You text someone, and they don't answer. You text again. After a while, you stop sending; silence is its own reply. So here's the odd detail. Elie Wiesel survived the Nazi camps as a boy, and spent his life writing so that what he saw would not be erased. In those books he keeps addressing God, with questions that are angry, raw and unanswered. If God felt that silent, why keep sending? Why not just stop?
screen: `YOU STOP TEXTING A SILENT NUMBER.` → `A SURVIVOR WHO KEPT WRITING.` → `WHY KEEP ASKING?`

segments.voice: The puzzle has an old answer, and it starts in Genesis. God tells Abraham that Sodom will be destroyed. Abraham doesn't bow and leave. He argues. Would you sweep away the innocent with the guilty? Then the line that still startles readers: "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?" A man is cross-examining God, and haggling, from fifty innocent people down to ten. And the text never scolds him for asking. The Psalms do it too: "Awake, why sleepest Thou, O Lord?" That's a prayer in the Bible, shouting at a God who seems asleep. So when Wiesel asks, he is standing in a very old line. Here is the solution to the puzzle. Walking away is silence. Asking is still talking to someone. An angry question is a way of staying in the relationship, even when it hurts. And a witness has two jobs. First, to say plainly what happened, so it isn't forgotten. Second, to refuse a tidy explanation that would make it smaller. In his writing the questions don't get neat answers, and he doesn't pretend they do. That honesty is part of the testimony. A note for families: Wiesel's subject is the darkest chapter there is, and younger listeners may want a grown-up nearby when they read him. The witness asks, because asking is how the witness keeps faith with the dead, and with God.
screen: `ABRAHAM ARGUES FOR SODOM.` · `AWAKE, WHY SLEEPEST THOU?` · `ASKING IS STILL TALKING TO SOMEONE.` · `SAY WHAT HAPPENED. NO TIDY ANSWERS.` · then, large: `THE WITNESS ASKS.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and a scrap of paper. Write down one thing you saw this week that someone ought to know, said as plainly as you can, with no explanation attached. If a question comes with it, write the question underneath and leave it open. For the rest of the sit, read your two lines once more, slowly, and let them stand there, true and unfixed.
screen: `ONE THING YOU SAW.` · `SAID PLAINLY.` · `THE QUESTION, LEFT OPEN.`

segments.voice: The witness asks: Wiesel's way, and Abraham's before him. Say what happened, and keep putting the hard question to God.
Your line: arguing with God is Abraham's way of faith. An open question can still be faithful. Day one thousand six hundred forty, done.

screen: `DAY 1640 COUNTS.` → `LATER VOICES · 33 OF 40.` → `TOMORROW: A HUGE BOOK YOU CAN'T READ. WHO OPENED IT?`

howItsDone: On Yom HaShoah, Holocaust Remembrance Day, Jewish communities gather to remember, sometimes reading survivors' words aloud; arguing with God goes back to Abraham in Genesis 18.

fork.setup: a friend's dad died suddenly. she says, 'i keep yelling at God in my head. is that bad?' what fits the witness who asks?
options: tell her she's in old company: Abraham and the Psalms argue with God too.
tell her to stop until she's calm, since anger at God pushes faith away.

fork.reveal: Genesis and the Psalms keep angry questions inside the relationship. Wiesel's books leave them open. asking is a way of staying.
